name: Orange stick

lead: An orange stick is a thin wooden manicure stick with a pointed end and a flat or beveled end. The beveled end eases back softened cuticles and the point cleans under the nail edge, leaving nails looking tidy and evenly framed.

It is a basic grooming tool, valued because wood is gentler on nail skin than metal and cheap enough to discard. Results last until nails and cuticles regrow. No studies have examined orange sticks specifically.

paras: People typically soften their hands in warm water or apply cuticle oil, then gently press the cuticle back with the beveled end and clean under the free edge with the point. Sticks are sold in packs in beauty and drug stores and are used alongside clippers, files and cuticle products.

Hard pressure can tear skin or damage the area around the nail, and tools used on several people can carry infection; salons discard sticks after one client and some give them to clients to take home. Home sticks can last a few weeks with care.

angle.text: The stick tidies the cuticle line and nail edge so that hands look neat, usually after soaking or oiling. Because nails and cuticles keep growing, the effect lasts until the next manicure.

lead: An orange stick is a manicure tool: a thin wooden stick, usually 10 to 11 cm long, with a pointed end and a flat or beveled end. It is used to ease back cuticles and clean beneath the free edge of the nail, which makes the nail line look neat and the hands look groomed.

The name is traditionally explained by the tool's origin in orange-tree wood, with orange-colored sticks and packaging helping the name stick; many modern sticks use other woods.[1] Wikipedia's manicure article lists the orangewood stick among standard manicure implements and notes that some salons give clients wooden cuticle sticks to take home rather than reuse shared tools.[2]
No clinical research has examined orange sticks specifically.
infobox: Single use in salons; replaced when worn[1]

paras: Orange sticks typically have a pointed end for cleaning under the nail and detail work and a flat or beveled end for pushing back cuticles; some have two beveled ends.[1] Suppliers describe the wood as smooth and splinter-free, and the natural material as less irritating than metal tools.[1] Metal cuticle pushers serve a similar purpose and are also sold.

Manicurists push back and trim nonliving tissue at the cuticle with pushers and nippers and remove hangnails, often after softening the area with water or oils such as mineral or olive oil.[2] Supplier guidance recommends soaking the hands in warm water first so the cuticles soften.[1]

Because manicures can break or trim the skin, using the same tools on multiple clients can spread infection, and salons may offer personal tool kits to reduce the risk.[2] Professional guidance holds that wooden sticks should be discarded after one client, with nitrile or medical gloves worn; at home a stick can last for weeks if cared for.[1]
